A drunkard is a person who drinks alcohol excessively and repeatedly, as a fixed habit in their life. The key idea here is habit — not someone who occasionally drinks too much, but someone for whom drinking heavily is a regular, ongoing pattern of behavior.

Think of it this way: if a person gets drunk at one party, that does not make them a drunkard. But if drinking heavily is something they do again and again, day after day or week after week, and it has become a defining part of how they live — that person is a drunkard.
The two essential ideas packed into this word

To truly understand "drunkard," hold these two ideas together:

  1. Excess — They drink far more than is normal or healthy.
  2. Habit — This is not a one-time event. It is a repeated, ongoing behavior that has taken root in their life.

Remove either idea, and the word no longer applies. A single episode of getting drunk is not enough. And drinking a little every day is not enough either. It must be both — too much, and repeatedly.
The tone and attitude the word carries

"Drunkard" is not a neutral, descriptive word. It carries a strong negative judgment. When someone calls a person a drunkard, they are not simply reporting a fact — they are expressing disapproval, even contempt or moral criticism. The word implies that the person has a character flaw, a weakness, or a failure of self-control.

This makes it different from simply saying "he drinks a lot," which is more of a plain observation. Calling someone a drunkard is making a judgment about them as a person.

These words are related but are not identical:

Drunk (used as a noun, e.g., "he's a drunk"):
This is more casual and informal. It can mean someone who is currently intoxicated, or loosely refer to someone who drinks a lot. It does not carry as much weight or formality as "drunkard."

Alcoholic:
This is a medical and clinical term. It refers to someone who has a physical and psychological dependency on alcohol — a disease. It is largely neutral in tone, focused on the medical condition rather than moral judgment. A doctor or therapist would use this word.

Drunkard, by contrast, sits somewhere older and more moralistic. It emphasizes the behavior and the social or moral failing, rather than the medical condition. It feels like a word a preacher, a disapproving community, or an older generation might use.
The register: when and where this word appears

"Drunkard" has a somewhat old-fashioned or literary feel. You are more likely to encounter it in:

  • Classic literature and older novels
  • Religious texts or sermons (where it is used to warn against the sin of excessive drinking)
  • Formal writing
  • Historical contexts

In everyday modern conversation, people are more likely to say "he's a drunk," "she's an alcoholic," or "he has a drinking problem." "Drunkard" in casual modern speech can sound either deliberately dramatic, slightly poetic, or quaintly old-fashioned.
Example sentences to see it in action

• The old man had spent half his life as a drunkard, wasting his earnings at the tavern every night.
  • The village drunkard stumbled down the street, much to the shame of his family.
  • She had grown up watching her father, a hopeless drunkard, slowly destroy everything around him.
  • The preacher warned his congregation about the dangers of becoming a drunkard.

Notice how in each sentence, the word paints a picture not just of someone who drinks, but of someone whose drinking has become a defining characteristic — one that others see, judge, and are affected by.
The full picture in one sentence
A drunkard is a person who has made a habit of drinking alcohol to excess — and the word itself quietly announces that the speaker finds this behavior shameful, weak, or morally wrong.
